title: Chapter 5
paragraphs: At the concert that afternoon two very interesting pieces were performed. One was a fantasia, _King Lear;_ the other was a quartet dedicated to the memory of Bach. Both were new and in the new style, and Levin was eager to form an opinion of them. After seeing his sister-in-law to her seat, he stood against a column and tried to listen as attentively and conscientiously as he could. He tried not to let his attention be pulled away, and not to spoil his impression by looking at the conductor in his white tie, waving his arms — which always interfered so much with his enjoyment of music — or at the ladies in bonnets with the strings carefully tied over their ears, and all these people either thinking about nothing at all or thinking about every possible thing except the music. He tried to avoid running into musical experts or talkative acquaintances, and stood staring at the floor right in front of him, listening.

But the more he listened to the fantasia of _King Lear,_ the further he felt from forming any definite opinion of it. There was, as it were, a continual beginning, a preparation for some musical expression of feeling, and then it fell apart again immediately, breaking into new musical motifs — or into nothing but the composer's whims, sounds that were extremely complex but disconnected. And these fragmentary musical expressions, though sometimes beautiful, were unpleasant, because they came at you completely unexpectedly and were not led up to by anything. Cheerfulness and grief and despair and tenderness and triumph followed one another with no connection at all, like the emotions of a madman. And those emotions, like a madman's, sprang up out of nowhere.

Throughout the performance Levin felt like a deaf man watching people dance, and was in a state of complete bewilderment when the fantasia was over, and felt a great weariness from the fruitless strain on his attention. Loud applause broke out on all sides. Everyone stood up, milled about, started talking. Eager to throw some light on his own confusion using the impressions of others, Levin began walking around looking for connoisseurs, and was glad to see a well-known musical amateur talking with Pestsov, whom he knew.

"Marvelous!" Pestsov was saying in his mellow bass. "How are you, Konstantin Dmitrievitch? Particularly sculptural and plastic, so to speak, and richly colored is that passage where you feel Cordelia approaching — where woman, _das ewig Weibliche,_ comes into conflict with fate. Isn't it?"
"You mean ... what does Cordelia have to do with it?" Levin asked timidly, forgetting that the fantasia was supposed to depict King Lear.
"Cordelia comes in ... look here!" said Pestsov, tapping his finger on the satin surface of the program he was holding and handing it to Levin.
Only then did Levin remember the title of the fantasia, and he hurried to read in the Russian translation the lines from Shakespeare printed on the back of the program.
"You can't follow it without this," Pestsov said to Levin, since the person he had been talking to had walked off and he had no one else to talk to.

During the _entr'acte_ Levin and Pestsov fell into an argument about the merits and defects of music of the Wagner school. Levin held that the mistake of Wagner and all his followers was in trying to push music into the territory of another art, just as poetry goes wrong when it tries to paint a face the way painting is supposed to. As an example of this mistake he cited the sculptor who had carved in marble certain poetic phantoms hovering around the figure of a poet on a pedestal. "These phantoms were so far from being phantoms that they were positively clinging to the ladder," said Levin. The comparison pleased him, but then he could not remember whether he had used the same phrase before — and to Pestsov, too — and as he spoke it he felt awkward.
Pestsov maintained that art is one, and that it can reach its highest expressions only by joining together every kind of art.

The second piece on the program Levin could not really listen to. Pestsov, standing next to him, was talking to him almost the entire time, criticizing the music for its excessive, affected pretense of simplicity, and comparing it to the simplicity of the Pre-Raphaelites in painting. On the way out Levin ran into many more acquaintances, with whom he talked about politics, music, and people they both knew. Among others he met Count Bol, whom he had completely forgotten to call on.
"Well, go right now then," Madame Lvova said when he told her; "perhaps they won't be at home, and then you can come to the meeting to fetch me. You'll still find me there."
